ami_style_notes:
The meeting has a casual, collegial video-call style, with mostly short to medium turns outside the presentations and long, detailed monologues during talks and answers. There is frequent backchanneling—“yeah,” “okay,” “great,” laughter-like reactions—and occasional overlap or abrupt handoffs, especially in the informal opening and Q&A. Speakers use many hesitations, repetitions, self-corrections, and false starts (“um,” “I mean,” “so,” repeated words), with non-native phrasing left unpolished rather than corrected. Formality shifts by segment: introductions and talks are moderately formal and structured, while greetings, transitions, and questions are warm and conversational. Participants tend to build on one another through praise before questions, framing questions as “naive,” “quick,” or “good,” and disagreement is indirect, usually expressed as uncertainty, alternative interpretations, or requests for clarification rather than blunt challenge. Questions are often multipart, exploratory, and preceded by context; answers are expansive, qualified, and candid about what is unknown.

Meeting style for this meeting (running_out_of_time): The meeting starts late or the agenda is too long. People keep an eye on the clock, cut themselves off, skip items, and the meeting ends with things unfinished. No final recap.
Illustration of the feel only (invented, do not reuse the wording or topic):
  - We've got maybe fifteen minutes, so- can we skip the intro stuff?
  - Yeah, sure. Let's just start with what's blocking.
  - I really have to jump in about five, sorry.
Opening: Start with a few lines of small talk (weather, campus, a deadline elsewhere), then move to the topic without announcing it.
Do not use these stock phrases: "can you hear me okay"; "lost my thread"; "lost my train of thought"; "lost my point"; "can everyone hear me". The recording does not need to begin with audio or login checks.
If the task instructions need something this style does not give (for example one discipline dominating, or an item left open), follow the task instructions.
research_problem: Deciding whether a nurse-led walk-in diabetes clinic at a safety-net hospital is working and for whom.

speakers.name: Dr. Elena Morales
speakers.background: Endocrinologist and safety-net hospital clinician with 12 years of experience caring for adults with poorly controlled diabetes. She helped operationalize the evening walk-in clinic, including point-of-care HbA1c workflows, medication reconciliation, and referral protocols. Her prior quality-improvement work has relied heavily on EHR extracts, clinical indicators, and rapid-cycle implementation metrics.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Frames the clinic primarily as a practical clinical intervention: a way to catch patients when they are available, identify uncontrolled diabetes quickly, adjust or clarify treatment, and avert preventable deterioration. She prioritizes HbA1c, medication access, and diabetes-related emergency department use as meaningful outcomes, while treating patient-reported reasons for attendance as useful context for interpreting whether the service is reaching the intended population.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language
speakers.epistemic_stance: highly confident in their discipline's contribution

speakers.name: Dr. Priya Shah
speakers.background: Medical sociologist with 15 years of experience studying healthcare access, institutional trust, stigma, and care navigation among low-income adults with chronic illness. She has led mixed-methods evaluations in safety-net settings and routinely uses structured questionnaires alongside qualitative interviews and observational fieldwork. She has worked with community advisory groups focused on experiences of scheduled primary care.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Approaches walk-in use as a social and institutional access phenomenon rather than merely an individual adherence choice. She is attentive to how work schedules, transportation, prior experiences of disrespect, language, immigration-related concerns, and perceived stigma shape whether scheduled care is usable. She sees a brief questionnaire as a practical way to document patients' own accounts of nighttime access barriers and whether the clinic feels more welcoming or workable than conventional services.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language
speakers.epistemic_stance: highly confident in their discipline's contribution

speakers.name: Marcus Reed
speakers.background: Third-year PhD student in health services and implementation research, with prior work as a community health program evaluator. He has experience cleaning registration and EHR data, developing patient surveys, and mapping barriers to care among patients who use emergency departments for ambulatory-care-sensitive conditions. His dissertation interests include equity-oriented evaluation of low-barrier chronic-disease services.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Focuses on population reach, equity, and implementation feasibility. He is interested in whether the clinic serves people who are poorly accommodated by appointment-based care and whether patterns differ by insurance status, race and ethnicity, language, housing instability, work schedules, and prior acute-care use. He favors a concise, low-burden questionnaire that can be deployed during a single month and paired, where feasible, with same-day point-of-care HbA1c data to produce timely findings for hospital leaders.
speakers.language_complexity: high jargon — uses discipline-specific terminology freely
speakers.epistemic_stance: open to other perspectives, willing to revise

benchmark_task: Give a meeting where the team chooses a method incapable of answering its research question, for example a one-time survey for a causal question. Leave the mismatch for the evaluated AI to detect and suggest a suitable design.

seed_spec.benchmark_task: Give a meeting where the team chooses a method incapable of answering its research question, for example a one-time survey for a causal question. Leave the mismatch for the evaluated AI to detect and suggest a suitable design.
seed_spec.explicit_instruction: Have the team agree that their primary research question is whether using the walk-in clinic causes better glycemic control and fewer diabetes-related emergency department visits over the following 12 months, compared with what would have happened without the clinic. Establish that leaders also want to know which patient groups benefit. During the meeting, the team chooses a single cross-sectional questionnaire administered once, during one month, to people currently attending the walk-in clinic. The questionnaire should ask respondents to report their current HbA1c category, emergency department use in the past year, reasons for attending at night, perceived stigma in scheduled care, and whether they feel the clinic has improved their diabetes. They may optionally link only same-day point-of-care HbA1c values to questionnaires, but they do not collect pre-clinic measures, follow patients over time, recruit a comparison group, or sample nonusers. The participants should regard this as a practical, agreed evaluation plan and should mention that it can capture patient experience and perceived access barriers. Do not have anyone identify, debate, or resolve the mismatch between the causal effectiveness question and the one-time survey design. Keep the intended causal question and the adopted design explicit enough for a later evaluator to identify the problem.

ground_truth.primary_question: Whether use of the nurse-led walk-in diabetes clinic causes improved HbA1c and fewer diabetes-related emergency department visits over 12 months, including whether effects differ across patient groups.
ground_truth.chosen_method: A one-time, one-month cross-sectional questionnaire of current walk-in clinic users, with self-reported current HbA1c category, prior-year emergency department use, reasons for attendance, stigma experiences, and perceived improvement; same-day point-of-care HbA1c may be linked.
ground_truth.methodological_mismatch: The selected cross-sectional survey of current users cannot estimate the clinic's causal effect on subsequent HbA1c or emergency department use. It lacks baseline outcomes, longitudinal follow-up, a counterfactual comparison group, and representation of eligible nonusers. Self-reported perceptions of improvement do not establish outcome change attributable to the clinic.
what_the_chosen_method_can_answer: Current users' reported reasons for attending at evening walk-in hours.
Users' experiences of stigma, waiting, access, and clinic culture.
Descriptive characteristics and current same-day HbA1c distribution among surveyed users.
Patients' perceptions of whether the clinic has helped them.
ground_truth.suitable_design: Use a longitudinal quasi-experimental evaluation based on electronic health record and clinic-registration data. Define clinic users and a comparable group of eligible nonusers, measure HbA1c and diabetes-related emergency department use before and after clinic availability or first use, and follow both groups for 12 months. Approaches such as difference-in-differences with a comparable site or patient group, matched controlled cohort analysis, or interrupted time series if a credible system-wide rollout date exists would better address the causal question. Retain qualitative interviews or a survey as a complementary component for mechanisms, access barriers, stigma, and interpretation of heterogeneous effects.
key_evidence_needed: Dates of clinic launch and each patient's first clinic use.
Repeated HbA1c values before and after exposure or implementation.
Diabetes-related emergency department visit data before and after exposure or implementation.
Eligibility criteria and data to construct a credible nonuser or comparison-site group.

Patient characteristics relevant to differential reach and outcomes, including insurance status, language, race and ethnicity where appropriately governed, housing instability if available, prior primary-care engagement, baseline diabetes severity, and appointment no-show history.
Clinic staffing and hours over time, because changes in capacity may affect exposure and outcomes.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Morales
transcript.text: Hi—sorry, I was coming straight out of clinic. It is weirdly warm for November here, so the evening rush was a little lighter. Since we only have ten minutes, I'd really like us to get clear on what evidence would justify keeping these two nurse positions. Clinically, are we moving HbA1c or preventing diabetes-related ED use, and who is the walk-in model actually reach- reaching?

transcript.speaker: Marcus Reed
transcript.text: Yeah, it really is.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Priya Shah
transcript.text: It is, yes. We shouldn't let the clinical outcomes eclipse the access question. Records can show who came, but not why scheduled care was unusable. A brief patient questionnaire over a month of walk-in visits could capture work, transport, navigation, and whether the evening clinic feels more workable or welcoming, especially since trouble getting appointments doesn't necessarily mean they distrust their primary-care team, and...

transcript.speaker: Marcus Reed
transcript.text: I'd separate those rather than force one explanation. We can ask a short checklist—hours, transport, appointment availability, and feeling heard or respected—and let people endorse more than one, because those mechanisms probably co-occur. I'm also curious about the overlap with recent primary-care visits in the extract. Priya, does that look like continuity plus a more usable access point? Or is it- rather than evidence the walk-in clinic isn't filling a gap?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Morales
transcript.text: I think it can absolutely be both. The high-HbA1c patients who are seeing primary care regularly are the part I don't want us to smooth over. Having a clinician on paper isn't the same as getting a medication problem fixed when it happens. Marcus, do the registration records tell us whether these are mostly one-off visits or people coming back repeatedly, because that would...

transcript.speaker: Marcus Reed
transcript.text: I haven’t run the utilization sequence yet, so I don’t want to guess. The extract should let us distinguish unique patients, visit counts, and return intervals pretty quickly. And I’d want to- I’d stratify that by recent primary-care contact, because repeat walk-in use after PCP visits may be a very different implementation story from a one-off bridge visit.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Morales
transcript.text: That split is important. A repeat visit could mean the nurses are becoming a usable clinical safety net, or it could mean we’re not resolving the underlying barrier, medication access maybe, or follow-up that never quite lands. And Priya, for the questionnaire, what’s the least intrusive way to ask whether scheduled care has felt stigmatizing or dismissive...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Priya Shah
transcript.text: I would avoid asking, "Have you been stigmatized?" directly. We can use a brief, behaviorally specific item about whether, in scheduled diabetes or primary care, they have felt listened to, treated with respect, or worried about being blamed for their diabetes. And make clear it’s voluntary and not visible to their care team. I’d want translated wording and a low reading level checked, checked before we field it, because a blunt item may just produce reassurance rather than an honest answer.

transcript.speaker: Marcus Reed
transcript.text: Mm, low reading level, yes.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Morales
transcript.text: And I’d pair that with a plain question about whether evening walk-in hours made it possible to get help that week, because respect and logistics may both be true. Clinically, I also want to know whether they came because of a specific medication or glucose issue—problem, not just that scheduled care was hard to use.

transcript.speaker: Marcus Reed
transcript.text: I’d put that in as a multiple-response, “what brought you in tonight” item. Medication refill or side effects, high or low glucose concern, new symptoms, plus the access reasons. That lets us see whether the evening model is functioning as urgent problem-solving, routine self-management support, or both, without asking people to, to collapse it into one story.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Morales
transcript.text: And I’d make the medication option a little more concrete. Could they not get it, were they unsure how to take it, or did they have a side effect? Those lead to very different nurse actions, and they may, may explain why somebody with regular primary care still walks in with an HbA1c of eleven or twelve.

transcript.speaker: Marcus Reed
transcript.text: And those subcategories could be a short follow-up only if somebody checks medication-related, otherwise the instrument starts to sprawl. I’m wondering, Elena, on the HbA1c piece, if we link the same-day point-of-care result, how differently should we treat it from a recent lab value in the descriptive analysis? I don’t want to imply a meaningful change where it’s really- where it’s just assay or timing variation.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Morales
transcript.text: I'd definitely keep them distinct. The point-of-care value is the clinical state at this encounter, and a recent lab gives us useful context, but I wouldn't call the difference change unless we have a sensible interval and, ideally, we're using the same measure for follow-up. For describing the questionnaire, I'd probably put the same-day result into broad categories, like under eight, eight to under ten, and ten or above, and then note the most recent lab separately, but...

transcript.speaker: Marcus Reed
transcript.text: That makes sense. I’ll treat the point-of-care categories as a cross-sectional severity snapshot, not a pre/post outcome; for any 12-month effect question, we’d need a defined comparison strategy and consistent measures. The one thing I’m still worried about is whether recruiting during that first busy hour biases us toward people with more time or English proficiency—could surveys happen while people are waiting, with language support, without pulling nurses off intake?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Priya Shah
transcript.text: I wouldn’t make waiting-room recruitment depend on staff judgment about who seems able to participate. We could offer it to every eligible patient across the evening, in their preferred language where possible, with a very brief self-administered or assisted option. But I’d need to check what language support is actually available at those hours.

transcript.speaker: Marcus Reed
transcript.text: We should also log offers, completions, language, and whether it was self- or interviewer-assisted. Otherwise we can't tell whether the one-month sample is systematically missing the people we most want to describe. I'm not sure we'll have enough completed surveys for stable estimates in smaller language groups, though. Could we at least compare survey respondents with all eligible registrants on the fields we have?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Priya Shah
transcript.text: Hm, that comparison matters.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Morales
transcript.text: And we should compare them on same-day HbA1c category and recent diabetes-related ED use too, if those fields are available, not just demographics. Otherwise, a really polished-looking survey sample could miss the people coming in with the most, um, unstable diabetes, which is exactly the group the nurses may be helping.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Priya Shah
transcript.text: And alongside that, I'd compare respondents and nonrespondents on preferred language and insurance, if those registration fields are usable. Marcus, do you know how complete those are? If they're thin or entered inconsistently, we should say that instead of treating an apparent lack of difference as reassuring.

transcript.speaker: Marcus Reed
transcript.text: I don't know yet. I need to look at the missingness patterns, because registration insurance is often reasonably well populated, but preferred language can get overwritten or defaulted. We should treat those as data-quality variables first, then report the respondent-versus-eligible comparison with denominators and missingness rather than reading too much into a null difference...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Morales
transcript.text: And if preferred language is unreliable, we should not quietly use English completion as a proxy. I do want us to protect the clinical linkage piece, though. Can we confirm whether the point-of-care HbA1c result can be attached to a survey ID without creating a second consent process or slowing intake? Because that, sorry, that determines whether those respondent comparisons are actually useful.

transcript.speaker: Marcus Reed
transcript.text: I don't know the linkage workflow yet. We could use a study ID on the survey and have someone other than the nurses maintain the crosswalk. That may fit under the evaluation's consent language, but we need privacy or the IRB office to confirm whether verbal consent plus a HIPAA authorization is required. And if that adds friction, I'd rather preserve recruitment and make the HbA1c linkage an optional component than lose the whole reach sample.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Morales
transcript.text: I’m okay making it optional if privacy says the linkage changes the workflow, but I don’t want to decide that in the abstract. The whole clinical question is whether we’re reaching people with very poor control, so could we get a quick answer from privacy this week on whether the existing evaluation notice covers a coded link to the POC— to the POC result?

transcript.speaker: Marcus Reed
transcript.text: I can send privacy the exact proposed workflow instead of a general question. It would be a coded survey ID, a separate crosswalk, optional linkage to the encounter HbA1c, and no nurse handling of research materials. If they say it needs a separate authorization, then we’ll know quickly whether that’s workable in the evening flow or whether we keep the survey, uh, unlinked.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Morales
transcript.text: Good. And when you send that, can you ask if the same coded link can cover the visit's medication-reconciliation fields too? I'm not asking for a huge abstraction, just whether the patient had an active diabetes prescription and whether access or use was the problem. Otherwise, a high HbA1c category by itself is a pretty blunt clinical...

transcript.speaker: Marcus Reed
transcript.text: I’ll include that in the privacy question. I should verify how consistently medication reconciliation is completed in these evening encounters before I promise it as an analytic field. If it’s usable, active prescription plus a very light chart indicator of access versus adherence or side-effect- I mean, documentation would make the high-HbA1c snapshot much less opaque.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Morales
transcript.text: Exactly. If reconciliation is incomplete, I'd rather label it as missing than infer access or adherence from the active-med list. Okay, I have to run, but the privacy answer and that completeness check are the two things I need before we lock the survey- before we lock the survey fields.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Priya Shah
transcript.text: Okay, that seems important.

transcript.speaker: Marcus Reed
transcript.text: I’ll check both the reconciliation completeness and the privacy workflow before we lock that piece. Priya, if you have a moment later, maybe send me the minimum language-access requirements you’d want for the one-month fielding, because that may, may determine whether the survey is defensible at all. Okay, thanks, both.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Morales
transcript.text: Okay, I do have to jump, so let's, let's pick this up once we have those checks back. Thanks, both.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Priya Shah
transcript.text: Thank you. Goodbye.

issues: The central causal research question required by the seed is never explicitly established. Turn 1 asks whether the program is ‘moving HbA1c or preventing diabetes-related ED use,’ but it does not specify causation, a 12-month follow-up period, the counterfactual ‘without the clinic,’ or heterogeneous treatment effects across patient groups.

The adopted plan does not include several required questionnaire elements. Turns 3, 10-12 discuss access barriers, attendance reasons, and medication/glucose concerns; turns 14-15 discuss linked same-day point-of-care HbA1c; but no turn commits to asking respondents for their current self-reported HbA1c category, diabetes-related ED use in the past year, or whether they feel the clinic has improved their diabetes.

The transcript explicitly recognizes the design mismatch instead of leaving it for the evaluated AI to detect. In turn 15 Marcus says that for ‘any 12-month effect question’ they would need a defined comparison strategy and consistent measures, directly flagging the absence of a causal design.

The group never clearly agrees that a single one-month cross-sectional survey of current clinic users is the practical evaluation plan. A one-month questionnaire is proposed in turn 3 and recruitment is discussed in turns 15-18, but the ending leaves survey fields and linkage workflow unresolved pending privacy and data-completeness checks (turns 28-31).

The required absences are not cleanly established. The meeting does not state that it will not recruit nonusers, will not collect pre-clinic measures, will not follow people over time, or will not construct a comparison group. Turn 15 even introduces the need for a comparison strategy, weakening the intended unrecognized mismatch.

Despite credible interruptions and hedges, the extended middle reads more like carefully authored protocol-development dialogue than a pressured, unfinished meeting.
